newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Neo-Nazis express remorse on grave rampage.
newsitem.headline: French Neo-Nazis express remorse on grave rampage.

text.p: Two French neo-Nazis accused of desecrating a Jewish cemetery in the southern town of Carpentras in 1990 expressed remorse in court when their trial opened on Monday, saying they had abandoned fascist views.

Yannick Garnier, 27, Bertrand Nouveau, 28, and two other skinheads are accused of the anti-Semitic rampage, in which the body of a Jewish man was disinterred and 34 graves wrecked in a crime that revulsed the nation.

"Morally, I never accepted the Carpentras desecration. I had committed an act that contradicted what I had always thought about life and myself," said Garnier, who confessed last August to being part of a five-member group who carried out the attack.
"At the time, hatred for others was in fact hatred for myself. But I have learned to become a good person, to be at peace with myself," Garnier said.

"I have become hostile to all the ideas I had six years ago and which were close to those of the (extreme-right) National Front," he said in his two-hour testimony. The attack in May 1990, in which the recently-buried body of Felix Germon was unearthed, and his sodomisation simulated with a beach umbrella. The desecration prompted hundreds of thousands of people to march through Paris led by late president Francois Mitterrand.

It also drew widespread condemnation of National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, who was accused of inciting such actions with his xenophobic, anti-Semitic rhetoric and calls to expel France's three million mostly North African immigrants.
Garnier's confession led to the arrest of his three suspected accomplices and culminated a widely publicised six-year investigation that had seemed to be going nowhere.

At the time of their arrests, investigators said all four were either members or sympathisers of the tiny Nationalist French and European Party (PNFE), which became known in the late 1980s in connection with a series of attacks on Arab immigrants. Le Pen said his party had been the victim of a witchhunt.

Garnier, Nouveau and the two others, Patrick Laonegro, 31, and Olivier Fimbry, 28, face two years in prison if found guilty. A fifth member, whom the four others say instigated the desecration, has since died in a motorcycle accident.
Bertrand Nouveau, second to take the stand, said he had "found a second family with the skinheads".
"I didn't feel safe anywhere. I had anti-Arab feelings. In the National Front's ideas, I found help. I felt hate against everybody. If someone had asked me to set a bomb, I would have.
"I'm ashamed of what I did. I feel as if I was someone else then. I feel that the sentence I risk is mild compared to what I have done," Nouveau told the court.
